instructions: Up to 2 days ahead: steep the tea bag in 1/3 cup boiling water for 5 minutes, then remove the bag. Pour the tea into a small saucepan with the prunes.
Simmer the prunes over medium-low heat until most of the tea is absorbed. Cover and let them cool.
Heat the oven to 400°F. Use 1 tbsp of the butter to grease a 6 cup (1.5 liter) baking dish well.

Put the remaining 4 tbsp butter in a light colored saucepan over medium-low heat. Cook it, swirling now and then, until the milk solids turn golden brown and it smells nutty. Take the pan off the heat and let the butter cool.
In a large bowl, whisk the flour, sugar and salt together.
Make a well in the middle, add the eggs, and whisk, drawing in flour from the edges, until smooth.
Whisk in the milk a little at a time, then the vanilla.
Whisk in the cooled brown butter.
Scatter the prunes over the bottom of the dish.
Pour the batter through a fine sieve over the prunes.
Bake for 35 to 45 minutes, until it's risen and deep golden, with a slight wobble in the center. Cool it for at least 20 minutes.
Serve slightly warm or at room temperature. Cover and refrigerate leftovers for up to 3 days, and slice them cold. Don't freeze it.
advance_prep_notes: The prunes can be simmered up to 2 days ahead, and the baked far keeps 3 days in the fridge.
method_notes: Sunday Baker (the lead, 4.6 from 12 ratings) uses a thin batter of flour, sugar, eggs and milk with browned butter, poured over simmered prunes and baked at 400°F; it is also where the 3 day fridge keeping time comes from. Brittany Tourism and The French Cooking Academy agree on the prunes under a thin custard batter but use more milk and a lower oven. The sources soak the prunes in brandy or rum; this one uses strong tea, the alcohol free option Sunday Baker names. The lead has fewer than 20 ratings, so this is a fallback lead. It makes a full dish, about 8 slices.
